Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. derivations.claim: For Hermitian $A,B$, $\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{Tr}((AB)^*)=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ by [F2]. The trace is additive and real-homogeneous, so the pairing is real-valued, symmetric, and real-bilinear.

Diagonalize $A\in\mathsf H_d$ by [F3] with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$. Then $\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)=\sum_j\lambda_j^2\ge0$, with equality exactly when all $\lambda_j=0$, hence exactly when $A=0$. This proves positive definiteness and the displayed square-root formula.

For $c\in\mathbb R^m$, bilinearity gives $c^\mathsf T Gc=\operatorname{Tr}((Sc)^2)=\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\ge0$. For $X\in\mathsf H_d$, the vector $v$ with coordinates $v_a=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aX)$ satisfies $\langle Sc,X\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}=c^\mathsf Tv$ for every $c$, so it is $S^*X$. By [F2], $v_a=\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)$; hence the matrix of $S^*S$ is precisely $G$. The equality $\langle c,Gc\rangle=\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$ implies $\ker G=\ker S$: $Sc=0$ gives $Gc=0$, while $Gc=0$ gives $\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2=0$ and hence $Sc=0$ by step 2.1. By [F4], $|\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$; expanding $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$ and applying this bound gives $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$. Thus the formula is a norm.

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

derivations.claim: Summing the product law [A1] over the other $n-1$ coordinates gives $\mathbb P(X_k=1)=p\prod_{j\ne k}(p+(1-p))=p$, so $\mathbb E X_k=p$. Put $S=\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-p)$. By [F1], $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(X_k-p)}\le e^{\lambda^2/8}$ for every real $\lambda$. Expanding the finite expectation over $\{0,1\}^n$ and using [A1] factors it into the product of these $n$ expectations. Hence $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S}\le e^{n\lambda^2/8}$.

For $\lambda>0$, $S\ge nt$ implies $e^{\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda nt}$. For any nonnegative $W$ and $c>0$, $W\ge c\,\mathbf1_{\{W\ge c\}}$, so $\mathbb P(W\ge c)\le\mathbb EW/c$. Apply this to $W=e^{\lambda S}$ and then step 1.1 to get $\mathbb P(f-p\ge t)\le e^{-\lambda nt+n\lambda^2/8}$. Setting $\lambda=4t$ gives $e^{-2nt^2}$.

Apply the same argument to $-S$, using step 1.1 at $-4t$; it gives $\mathbb P(p-f\ge t)\le e^{-2nt^2}$. The union bound follows from $\mathbf1_{A\cup B}\le\mathbf1_A+\mathbf1_B$, so adding the two tails proves the claim. A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\ge1$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]), with adjoints as in [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]] and the finite trace as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Recall that an endomorphism $F$ is an **effect** when $F\ge0$ and $I-F\ge0$, i.e. $0\le F\le I$ in the quadratic-form order ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]).

(a) *Definitions.* A finite POVM is a finite family $(F_a)_{a=1}^p$, $p\ge1$, of effects with $\sum_aF_a=I$. An **instrument** here is a finite family $(M_{a,r})_{1\le a\le p,\,1\le r\le q_a}$ of endomorphisms of $H$, where each $q_a$ is a non-negative integer; its outcome operators and update maps are $F_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ and $I_a:\operatorname{End}(H)\to\operatorname{End}(H)$, $I_a(R):=\sum_rM_{a,r}RM_{a,r}^*$, with empty sums equal to zero. It is **normalized** when $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I$. For a normalized instrument the $F_a$ are its **outcome effects**, as proved in (b); without normalization they need not be effects.

(b) If $(F_a)$ is a finite POVM and $\rho$ a density operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) then $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)\ge0$ and $\sum_ap_a=1$. If $(M_{a,r})$ is a normalized instrument then the $F_a$ form a finite POVM, $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=p_a$, each $I_a(\rho)$ is non-negative, and whenever $p_a>0$ the normalized update $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator.

(c) *Ideal Lüders case.* For an orthogonal projection $P$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]) put $M_0=P$, $M_1=I-P$. Then $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=P+(I-P)=I$, the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$, and $I_j(\rho)=P\rho P$ or $(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

(d) *Non-determination.* Effects alone do not determine the update: there are two normalized instruments on $\mathbb C^2$ with the same outcome effects $F_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $F_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ whose updates differ on the same input.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: Suppose all $P_i$ commute with all $Q_j$. Then $G_{ij}=P_iQ_j$ is self-adjoint, since $(P_iQ_j)^*=Q_jP_i=P_iQ_j$, and is idempotent, since $(P_iQ_j)^2=P_i^2Q_j^2=P_iQ_j$. For any $x$, $\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle=\langle G_{ij}x,G_{ij}x\rangle\ge0$, so each is positive; the sum identity makes each bounded above by $I_H$. Finite summation gives $\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}=(\sum_iP_i)(\sum_jQ_j)=I_H$, and the two marginal sums are $P_i$ and $Q_j$. So this family is a joint POVM.

Conversely, suppose a joint POVM $(G_{ij})$ exists. For each pair, $0\le G_{ij}\le P_i$ because $P_i-G_{ij}=\sum_{k\ne j}G_{ik}\ge0$, and similarly $0\le G_{ij}\le Q_j$. If $x\in\ker P_i$, then $0\le\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle\le\langle P_ix,x\rangle=0$. By [F2], $\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle=\|G_{ij}^{1/2}x\|^2$, hence $G_{ij}x=0$ and $G_{ij}(I-P_i)=0$. Taking adjoints gives $(I-P_i)G_{ij}=0$, so $G_{ij}=P_iG_{ij}P_i$. The same argument yields $G_{ij}=Q_jG_{ij}Q_j$.

Using $P_i=\sum_kG_{ik}$ and $Q_j=\sum_\ell G_{\ell j}$, we obtain $P_iQ_j=\sum_kG_{ik}Q_j$. The support relation $G_{ik}=Q_kG_{ik}Q_k$ from step 1.2 makes every term with $k\ne j$ zero, and the $k=j$ term is $G_{ij}$. Therefore $P_iQ_j=G_{ij}$. Since $G_{ij}$ is self-adjoint, taking adjoints gives $Q_jP_i=G_{ij}=P_iQ_j$. This proves commutation and uniqueness.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$.

Equip $\mathbb R^m$ with the dot product $c^\mathsf Tb=\sum_{a=1}^m c_ab_a$. Here $S^*:\mathsf H_d\to\mathbb R^m$ denotes the adjoint relative to this dot product and the displayed trace pairing: it is characterized by $c^\mathsf T(S^*X)=\langle Sc,X\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}$ for every $c\in\mathbb R^m$ and $X\in\mathsf H_d$. The following lemma proves that the trace pairing is an inner product and that this adjoint exists as a well-defined linear map; it also establishes that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. A later A-page lemma identifies this finite pseudoinverse with its spectral formula.

If $G=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda P_\lambda$ is its finite spectral resolution, then $G^+=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Moreover, every $X\in\mathsf H_d$ is reconstructed by
$$
X=\sum_{a=1}^m\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)D_a.
$$
This holds for redundant families as well as bases; $G$ need not be invertible.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\ge1$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]), with adjoints as in [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]] and the finite trace as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Recall that an endomorphism $F$ is an **effect** when $F\ge0$ and $I-F\ge0$, i.e. $0\le F\le I$ in the quadratic-form order ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]).

(a) *Definitions.* A finite POVM is a finite family $(F_a)_{a=1}^p$, $p\ge1$, of effects with $\sum_aF_a=I$. An **instrument** here is a finite family $(M_{a,r})_{1\le a\le p,\,1\le r\le q_a}$ of endomorphisms of $H$, where each $q_a$ is a non-negative integer; its outcome operators and update maps are $F_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ and $I_a:\operatorname{End}(H)\to\operatorname{End}(H)$, $I_a(R):=\sum_rM_{a,r}RM_{a,r}^*$, with empty sums equal to zero. It is **normalized** when $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I$. For a normalized instrument the $F_a$ are its **outcome effects**, as proved in (b); without normalization they need not be effects.

(b) If $(F_a)$ is a finite POVM and $\rho$ a density operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) then $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)\ge0$ and $\sum_ap_a=1$. If $(M_{a,r})$ is a normalized instrument then the $F_a$ form a finite POVM, $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=p_a$, each $I_a(\rho)$ is non-negative, and whenever $p_a>0$ the normalized update $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator.

(c) *Ideal Lüders case.* For an orthogonal projection $P$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]) put $M_0=P$, $M_1=I-P$. Then $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=P+(I-P)=I$, the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$, and $I_j(\rho)=P\rho P$ or $(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

(d) *Non-determination.* Effects alone do not determine the update: there are two normalized instruments on $\mathbb C^2$ with the same outcome effects $F_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $F_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ whose updates differ on the same input.

Input integers $d,m\ge1$, a finite POVM $(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ on $\mathbb C^d$ that spans the real Hermitian matrices, and real frequencies $f_a\ge0$ with $\sum_af_a=1$. Form the Gram matrix $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$, compute its Moore–Penrose inverse $G^+$, set $D_a=\sum_b(G^+)_{ba}F_b$, and return
$$
X=\sum_{a=1}^m f_aD_a.
$$
All sums and matrices are finite. The output is Hermitian. The procedure does not project $X$ onto the positive cone, and it makes no positivity claim for finite frequency inputs.

Let $n\ge1$, $p\in[0,1]$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n:\Omega\to\{0,1\}$ be measurable on a probability space with
$$\mathbb P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_n=x_n)=\prod_{k=1}^n b_p(x_k)\quad\text{for every }(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n.$$
Here $b_p(1)=p$ and $b_p(0)=1-p$, including $p=0$ and $p=1$. Thus the variables have the stated independent Bernoulli product law. For their frequency $f=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and every $t>0$,
$$
\mathbb P(|f-p|\ge t)\le2e^{-2nt^2}.
$$
No axiom of choice is assumed.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with The reals form a totally ordered field,
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).

Let $\mathsf H_d$ be the real vector space of Hermitian $d\times d$ complex matrices from the preceding definition. The pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ is real-valued, symmetric, real-bilinear, and positive definite on $\mathsf H_d$. Its associated norm is $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. For every $m\ge1$ and finite family $F_1,\ldots,F_m\in\mathsf H_d$, the Gram matrix $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite, equals $S^*S$ for the synthesis map $S c=\sum_ac_aF_a$, and satisfies $\ker G=\ker S$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] with $H=\rho$. Then $\sum_ap_aD_a=\rho$, so [F3] gives $X(p)=\rho$. The probabilities are in $[0,1]$ and sum to one by [F2].

For each sample $k$, $\sum_{a=1}^m\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}=1$, so $f_a\ge0$ and $\sum_af_a=1$, as required by [F3]. Fix an outcome $a$ and set $Z_k^a=\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}$. For every $z\in\{0,1\}^n$, summing [A1] over the finite outcome tuples with $\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}=z_k$ gives $$\mathbb P(Z_1^a=z_1,\ldots,Z_n^a=z_n)=\prod_{k=1}^n\sum_{b:\,\mathbf1_{\{b=a\}}=z_k}p_b=\prod_{k=1}^n b_{p_a}(z_k),$$ since [F2] gives $\sum_bp_b=1$. Thus these indicators have the Bernoulli product law, and [F4] yields $\mathbb P(|f_a-p_a|\ge t)\le2e^{-2nt^2}$. No independence between indicators for different outcomes is used.

By the stated linear extension, $X(f)-\rho=D(f-p)$. Set $C=(\sum_a\|D_a\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2)^{1/2}$. By [F7], this is the norm from a real inner product, so its triangle inequality follows from [F5] by expanding the square of a sum. Thus $\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\sum_a|c_a|\|D_a\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le C\|c\|_2$. Since $m\ge1$, the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^m$ contains $e_1$, so the set $\{\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:\|c\|_2=1\}$ is nonempty; the bound makes it bounded above. Its supremum exists by [F6] and is the finite induced operator norm in the Statement. Scaling $c$ (and treating $c=0$ directly) gives $\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\|c\|_2$, which proves the deterministic estimate.

A finite union bound gives $\mathbb P(\exists a:\ |f_a-p_a|\ge t)\le2m e^{-2nt^2}$. Set $t=\sqrt{\log(2m/\delta)/(2n)}$, which is positive since $2m/\delta>1$; then the right side is $\delta$. On the complementary event, $\|f-p\|_2\le\sqrt m\,t$, and step 2.1 gives the asserted state-error bound.

Let $d,e\ge1$ and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A finite completely positive instrument from $\mathbb C^d$ to $\mathbb C^e$ is a family of completely positive complex-linear maps $I_a:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$, indexed by $a\in\mathcal A$, whose sum is trace-preserving. Then there are an integer $q\ge1$, an isometry $V:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e\otimes\mathbb C^q$, and pairwise orthogonal projections $Q_a$ on $\mathbb C^q$ with $\sum_aQ_a=I_q$ such that, for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$,
$$
I_a(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left[(I_e\otimes Q_a)VXV^*(I_e\otimes Q_a)\right].
$$
Here $E=\mathbb C^q$ is the finite register space with its displayed orthonormal basis, and the partial trace is defined on its matrix units by $\operatorname{Tr}_E(Y\otimes|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{b,s}|)=\delta_{(a,r),(b,s)}Y$, extended linearly. The register basis is indexed by the Kraus labels $(a,r)$; a zero outcome map has no labels and corresponds to $Q_a=0$.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

derivations.claim: Since $P_a^*=P_a=P_a^2$, the Lüders Kraus operators have $M^{L*}_aM^L_a=P_a$. For the other family, $M^{R*}_aM^R_a=(|a\rangle\langle+|)(|+\rangle\langle a|)=\langle+|+\rangle P_a=P_a$, since the displayed normalized vector satisfies $\langle+|+\rangle=1$. Thus both families are normalized, with the same outcome effects, because $P_0+P_1=I$.

By [F3], the one-operator Kraus forms give completely positive maps, and their sum is trace-preserving because the combined adjoint products sum to identity by step 1.1. Hence both are finite instruments in the sense of the A-page theorem, and each admits its stated outcome-register dilation by [F2].

On $\rho=P_0$, the Lüders update for outcome $0$ is $I^L_0(P_0)=P_0$, whereas the other update is $I^R_0(P_0)=|+\rangle\langle+|$. These matrices differ: $P_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $|+\rangle\langle+|=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. The outcome probabilities are nevertheless identical, $\operatorname{Tr}(P_0P_0)=1$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(P_0P_1)=0$. This refutes the statement.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\ge1$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]), with adjoints as in [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]] and the finite trace as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Recall that an endomorphism $F$ is an **effect** when $F\ge0$ and $I-F\ge0$, i.e. $0\le F\le I$ in the quadratic-form order ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]).

(a) *Definitions.* A finite POVM is a finite family $(F_a)_{a=1}^p$, $p\ge1$, of effects with $\sum_aF_a=I$. An **instrument** here is a finite family $(M_{a,r})_{1\le a\le p,\,1\le r\le q_a}$ of endomorphisms of $H$, where each $q_a$ is a non-negative integer; its outcome operators and update maps are $F_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ and $I_a:\operatorname{End}(H)\to\operatorname{End}(H)$, $I_a(R):=\sum_rM_{a,r}RM_{a,r}^*$, with empty sums equal to zero. It is **normalized** when $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I$. For a normalized instrument the $F_a$ are its **outcome effects**, as proved in (b); without normalization they need not be effects.

(b) If $(F_a)$ is a finite POVM and $\rho$ a density operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) then $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)\ge0$ and $\sum_ap_a=1$. If $(M_{a,r})$ is a normalized instrument then the $F_a$ form a finite POVM, $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=p_a$, each $I_a(\rho)$ is non-negative, and whenever $p_a>0$ the normalized update $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator.

(c) *Ideal Lüders case.* For an orthogonal projection $P$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]) put $M_0=P$, $M_1=I-P$. Then $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=P+(I-P)=I$, the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$, and $I_j(\rho)=P\rho P$ or $(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

(d) *Non-determination.* Effects alone do not determine the update: there are two normalized instruments on $\mathbb C^2$ with the same outcome effects $F_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $F_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ whose updates differ on the same input.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $d,m,n\ge1$, let $(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite POVM on $\mathbb C^d$ whose real span is $\mathsf H_d$, and let $\rho\in\mathsf H_d$ satisfy $\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_a)$, form the canonical dual $D_a$ from the Gram pseudoinverse, and write $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$ for $D c=\sum_ac_aD_a$.

Define the frequency simplex $\Delta_m=\{f\in\mathbb R^m:f_a\ge0\text{ for all }a,\ \sum_af_a=1\}$ and the real-linear map $X:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$ by $X(f)=\sum_af_aD_a$. On $\Delta_m$, this is the output of the previously defined linear-inversion procedure; on all of $\mathbb R^m$, $X$ denotes its linear extension. Use the induced operator norm $\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}=\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$.

Then exact probabilities reconstruct the state: $X(p)=\rho$. For every real frequency vector $f\in\mathbb R^m$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\|f-p\|_2.
$$
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be measurable with the independent product law $\mathbb P(Y_1=a_1,\ldots,Y_n=a_n)=\prod_kp_{a_k}$ for every outcome tuple. Define $f_a=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}$. Then for every $0<\delta<1$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le a\le m}|f_a-p_a|\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}\right)\ge1-\delta.
$$
Consequently, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\sqrt m\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}.
$$
These are conditional mathematical statements under the specified product sampling law; no empirical data or calibrated apparatus is asserted.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $F_1,\ldots,F_m\in\mathsf H_d$ span $\mathsf H_d$ over $\mathbb R$, and form $S$, $G=S^*S$, $G^+$, and $D_a$ as in the preceding finite-frame definition. If $G=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda P_\lambda$ is its finite spectral resolution, then $G^+=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Moreover, every $X\in\mathsf H_d$ is reconstructed by
$$

$$
This holds for redundant families as well as bases; $G$ need not be invertible.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$.

Equip $\mathbb R^m$ with the dot product $c^\mathsf Tb=\sum_{a=1}^m c_ab_a$. Here $S^*:\mathsf H_d\to\mathbb R^m$ denotes the adjoint relative to this dot product and the displayed trace pairing: it is characterized by $c^\mathsf T(S^*X)=\langle Sc,X\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}$ for every $c\in\mathbb R^m$ and $X\in\mathsf H_d$. The following lemma proves that the trace pairing is an inner product and that this adjoint exists as a well-defined linear map; it also establishes that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $\sigma_j^2=I$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j)=0$, $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, and $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$; reversing the order negates each mixed product. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}$. Since a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix has two real diagonal entries and one complex off-diagonal entry, $\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathsf H_2=4$; the four nonzero orthogonal matrices $I,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ form a basis. Every trace-one Hermitian $\rho$ therefore has the stated form with $r_j=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_j)\in\mathbb R$. Positivity [A2] restricts $|r|\le1$, since $(r_x\sigma_x+r_y\sigma_y+r_z\sigma_z)^2=|r|^2I$ and the eigenvalues of $\rho$ are $(1\pm|r|)/2$.

Each $\sigma_j$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $1,-1$ by step 1.1, so $F_{j,\pm}$ has eigenvalues $1/3,0$ and is positive. For each $j$, $F_{j,+}+F_{j,-}=I/3$; summing over $x,y,z$ gives $I$. Also $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, so each $\sigma_j$ lies in the real span of the effects. Since $I$ is their sum, the basis in step 1.1 shows that the effects span $\mathsf H_2$.

In the coordinate order $(x+,x-,y+,y-,z+,z-)$, direct multiplication and step 1.1 give $G_{(j,s),(k,t)}=\frac1{36}\operatorname{Tr}((I+s\sigma_j)(I+t\sigma_k))=\frac1{18}(1+st\,\delta_{jk})$ for $s,t\in\{+1,-1\}$. Thus the diagonal entries are $1/9$, opposite outcomes on one axis have entry $0$, and distinct axes have entry $1/18$. Let $u=(1,1,1,1,1,1)$ and $v_j=e_{j+}-e_{j-}$. Then $Gu=u/3$, $Gv_j=v_j/9$, and $G$ vanishes on vectors $(s_x,s_x,s_y,s_y,s_z,s_z)$ with $s_x+s_y+s_z=0$. These mutually orthogonal subspaces have dimensions $1,3,2$ and span $\mathbb R^6$.

By [F2] and the eigenspaces in step 3.1, $G^+=3P_u+9\sum_jP_{v_j}$, where $P_u=uu^\mathsf T/6$ and $P_{v_j}=v_jv_j^\mathsf T/2$. The $e_{j+}$ column of $G^+$ is $u/2+9v_j/2$. Applying the canonical-dual formula [F3], using $\sum_{k,\pm}F_{k,\pm}=I$ and $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, gives $D_{j,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_j$; similarly $D_{j,-}=\frac12I-\frac32\sigma_j$. The probabilities are $p_{j,\pm}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_{j,\pm})=(1\pm r_j)/6$, so $\sum_{j,\pm}p_{j,\pm}D_{j,\pm}=\frac12I+\frac12\sum_jr_j\sigma_j=\rho$, in agreement with [F1].

The frequency vector with $f_{x,+}=1$ and all other entries zero is nonnegative and sums to one. Its output is $D_{x,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_x$, whose eigenvalues are $2$ and $-1$. It is Hermitian but not positive, so the linear-inversion procedure does not preserve positivity for every frequency vector.
